Experiments that changed questions

The foot in the door: from a sticker to a huge sign

Those who agreed to a small favour were much more willing to agree to a large one later.

In 1966, Jonathan Freedman and Scott Fraser visited homes in Palo Alto, California, with an outsized request: to put up a large, unattractive "Drive Carefully" sign in the front garden. When asked directly, fewer than one in five households agreed.

Start small

Two weeks earlier, other households had been asked by someone else for something minimal: to put a small road-safety sticker in the window. Almost all agreed. When they were later asked about the large sign, about three in four agreed.

This is the foot-in-the-door technique. By agreeing to the first request, people start to see themselves as someone who supports that cause, and it is more consistent to keep doing so. Salespeople, charities and campaigns use it. Knowing about it helps you spot when a chain of small "yeses" is leading you somewhere you did not want to go.

References

  1. Freedman, J. L. y Fraser, S. C. (1966). Compliance without pressure: the foot-in-the-door technique. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 4(2), 195–202.
